Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette: Arthur Vance had been twenty-two when the mortar struck the ridge outside his forward operating base in the Helmand Valley. He was certain that the ground simply gave way, followed by a sky of shattered dust and the sharp, metallic cracks of incoming rounds. He remembered the heat pressing against his face, the sudden silence of the men beside him, and the heavy, wet guilt that settled in his chest as he pulled himself from the dirt. He had come to believe that surviving when others did not was a quiet betrayal. In the months that followed, that initial shock crystallized into a steady, unspoken terror. When he closed his eyes, the valley would rise again with all its original force, and the same terror that had once locked his knees would flood his body. He knew exactly what had happened, yet when his partner asked him to explain it, he would stare at the kitchen table, his mouth opening and closing as he could not find words to describe it. The days bled into years as Arthur built a life around the edges of that memory. He began to view the world as a dangerous place, a landscape where any sudden sound or shifting routine could unspool him. He stopped wearing the faded olive-drab field jacket he had kept from deployment, folding it away in a cedar chest while the fabric and cut still mirrored the uniform he had worn on the ridge. He refused to go near the specific valley where the strike occurred, telling himself it was merely a preference, though he would turn his truck a mile out of his way to pass that stretch of highway. Thinking about the event became something to be managed rather than faced; he would deliberately steer conversations toward the weather or the weathered work schedules on his breakroom bulletin board, keeping the heavy, unspoken past at bay. His identity felt untethered. He had come to believe that the man he was before the ridge no longer fit him, that he moved through his own life like a ghost wearing familiar skin. At his current job in a sprawling warehouse on the city's industrial edge, these habits took on concrete shape. Arthur worked the receiving bay, where the heavy canvas work boots he now wore daily echoed the tread of his old issue boots, and where the high metal racks and rolling steel doors mirrored the outpost's layout. When the bay doors clanged shut on a particularly hot afternoon, the sound caught in his throat, and he would stand perfectly still until the echo faded. His relationship had shifted around this quiet withdrawal; his partner had learned not to press him when he grew still during stories, nor to hang up the olive jacket on the back of the hallway chair where he could see it. Over the years, these avoided locations, the hidden jacket, and the careful management of his thoughts had accumulated into a life that felt carefully measured but narrowing. His relief work schedule had shortened, and he no longer volunteered for the overtime runs that took him past the valley exits. What finally brought Arthur to seek help was not a sudden crisis but a gradual suffocation. He sat in the waiting room with a manila folder on his lap, his hands resting on the worn denim of his trousers. He was most afraid that the quiet space around him was actually a trap, that he would one day find himself utterly alone with a memory he could not name. Yet, beneath the hesitation, there was a steady hope that someone might help him sort through the unspoken dust, that he might once again find the words without losing the peace he had fought to keep.
